The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Work over ZF. The **real dominated-extension principle**, denoted **HB**, is the following assertion:

For every real vector space $X$, every sublinear functional $p:X\to\mathbb R$ in the sense of [[def-sublinear-functional]], every real linear subspace $M\le X$ in the sense of [[def-linear-subspace]], and every real linear functional $g:M\to\mathbb R$ in the sense of [[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]],
$$\bigl(\forall m\in M,\ g(m)\le p(m)\bigr)\ \Longrightarrow\ \exists F:X\to\mathbb R\ \bigl(F\text{ is real linear},\ F|_M=g,\ \forall x\in X,\ F(x)\le p(x)\bigr).$$

This names an additional principle; it does not assert a proof of HB in ZF. Subsequent results explicitly state when they assume HB. Neither topology nor completeness is part of this assertion. The subspace may be $\{0\}$ or all of $X$. Sublinearity at scalar zero gives $p(0)=0$, and a linear functional has value zero at zero.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space and let $B$ be a real
separable Banach space with its norm Borel sigma-algebra. A map
$W:\Omega\to B$ is a **centered Borel Gaussian random element** if it is
Borel-measurable and, for every $\ell\in B^*$, the real random variable
$\ell(W)$ has a centered (possibly zero-variance) normal law. Its law is the
Borel probability $\mu=P\circ W^{-1}$. When the word *tight* is used, it means
that for every $\delta>0$ there is a norm-compact $K\subseteq B$ with
$\mu(K)>1-\delta$.

This definition concerns a random element in $B$. A Gaussian process on an
arbitrary index set with only a cylinder-space law does not satisfy it unless
a Borel $B$-valued realization is separately constructed.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume AC. Let $W$ be a centered Borel Gaussian random element in a real separable
Banach space $B$, with law $\mu$. For $\ell\in B^*$ define
$$C\ell=E[\ell(W)W]\in B,\qquad Q(\ell,m)=E[\ell(W)m(W)]\quad(\ell,m\in B^*).$$
The **Cameron–Martin reproducing-kernel Hilbert space** $H$ is the completion
of $B^*/N$ in the inner product induced by $Q$, where
$N=\{\ell\in B^*:Q(\ell,\ell)=0\}$. The canonical map sends the class of
$\ell$ to $C\ell$ and extends continuously to an injective map $i:H\to B$;
we identify $H$ with its image in $B$ and use the completed Hilbert norm
$\|\cdot\|_H$. The preceding construction is well-defined by
[[thm-banach-gaussian-covariance-rkhs-is-well-defined]].

The term *RKHS* here denotes this covariance-induced Hilbert space of shifts
inside $B$; it is not the space of all continuous functions on an arbitrary
index set.

Assume AC. Under the hypotheses and notation of
[[def-banach-gaussian-covariance-operator-and-rkhs]], each $C\ell$ exists as a
Bochner integral; $Q$ is a finite positive-semidefinite bilinear form;
$N=\{\ell:Q(\ell,\ell)=0\}$ is its nullspace; and the induced map from the
completion of $B^*/N$ to $B$ is continuous and injective. Thus the definition
identifies a Hilbert space of shifts in $B$.

Assume HB and countable choice. Let $B$ be a real separable Banach space. There is a sequence
$(\ell_j)_{j\ge1}\subseteq B^*$ with $\|\ell_j\|=1$ such that
$$\|x\|=\sup_{j\ge1}|\ell_j(x)|\qquad(x\in B).$$
If $B=\{0\}$, the conclusion is interpreted using the zero functional and the
supremum is $0$.

Assume AC. Let $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$ with positive-definite covariance
$\Sigma$. Let $L:\mathbb R^d\to[0,M]$ be Borel measurable and symmetric,
$L(-x)=L(x)$, and quasi-convex, meaning each sublevel set
$\{x:L(x)\le t\}$ is convex. Then for every $a\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$E L(X-a)\ge E L(X-m).$$
Thus the Gaussian center $m$ minimizes expected loss. The result includes
quasi-convex losses whose sublevel sets are not closed.

Let $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a decreasing sequence of measurable sets for a measure $\mu$. If $\mu(E_{n_0})<+\infty$ for some $n_0$, then

$$\mu\left(\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n\right)=\inf_{n\in\mathbb N}\mu(E_n).$$

Apply [F4] to the bounded loss $1_{D_n^c}$ in those coordinates: its sublevel sets are $D_n$ and the whole space, so it is symmetric and quasi-convex. This yields
$$ \mathbb P(Y_n-a_n\in Q_n)\le\mathbb P(Y_n\in Q_n). $$

Put $A_r=\overline B_B(0,r)$. By [F4], $\mu(A_r)>0$ because it contains the open ball of radius $r$ about the support point $0$. Let $(\ell_j)$ be the norming family from [F6], and define $A_{r,n}=\bigcap_{j\le n}\{|\ell_j(W)|\le r\}$. The sets decrease to $A_r$. For fixed $n$, the vector $(z_s,\ell_1(W),\ldots,\ell_n(W))$ is centered Gaussian: [F3] makes $z_s$ an $L^2$ limit of continuous-linear Gaussian coordinates, so adjoining the finitely many displayed coordinates gives a centered Gaussian limit. Its law is invariant under simultaneous sign reversal, and $A_{r,n}$ is invariant under that reversal. Hence
$$ \mathbb E[e^{z_s}\mathbf1_{A_{r,n}}]=\mathbb E[e^{-z_s}\mathbf1_{A_{r,n}}], \qquad \mathbb E[z_s\mathbf1_{A_{r,n}}]=0. $$
The variables $e^{\pm z_s}$ are integrable by the Gaussian moment formula in [F3]. Dominated convergence as $n\to\infty$ therefore gives conditional symmetry and conditional mean zero on $A_r$. Thus
$$ 1\le \mathbb E_\mu[e^{-z_s}\mid A_r]\le e^{\|s\|_E^2/2}. $$
For the lower bound, conditional Jensen applies. For the upper bound, [F3] applied to $-s$ gives
$$ \mathbb E_\mu[e^{-z_s}\mathbf 1_{A_r}] =e^{\|s\|_E^2/2}\,\mu(\overline B_B(is,r)), $$
and [F5] bounds the last probability by $\mu(A_r)$.

For any $h\in E$, choose $\ell_n\in B^*$ with $h_n:=C\ell_n\to h$ in $E$, possible by the completion in [F2], and put $s_n=h-h_n$. The Cameron–Martin formula [F3], applied to the translate by $-h$, gives
$$ \frac{\mu(\overline B_B(ih,r))}{\mu(A_r)} =e^{-\|h\|_E^2/2}\,\mathbb E_\mu[e^{-z_h}\mid A_r]. $$
Since $z_{h_n}=\ell_n(W)$ almost surely and $z_h=z_{h_n}+z_{s_n}$, the bound $|\ell_n(W)|\le r\|\ell_n\|_{B^*}$ on $A_r$ and step 1.1 imply
$$ e^{-r\|\ell_n\|_{B^*}} \le \mathbb E_\mu[e^{-z_h}\mid A_r] \le e^{r\|\ell_n\|_{B^*}}e^{\|s_n\|_E^2/2}. $$
For fixed $n$, let $r\downarrow0$; then let $n\to\infty$, so $\|s_n\|_E\to0$. The two bounds show $\mathbb E_\mu[e^{-z_h}\mid A_r]\to1$.

Applying step 1.2 separately to $h_1$ and $h_2$ yields
$$ \frac{\mu(\overline B_B(ih_1,r))}{\mu(\overline B_B(ih_2,r))} =e^{(\|h_2\|_E^2-\|h_1\|_E^2)/2} \frac{\mathbb E[e^{-z_{h_1}}\mid A_r]}{\mathbb E[e^{-z_{h_2}}\mid A_r]}. $$
Both conditional expectations tend to $1$, so the ratio has the stated limit. Positivity of the denominator follows from [F4], since each closed ball contains the corresponding open neighborhood of a support point.

Let $X$ be a specified real separable Banach or Hilbert parameter space with metric $d_X(x,x')=\|x-x'\|_X$ and its norm topology. Let $(Y,d_Y)$ be a metric data space equipped with a sigma-algebra $\Sigma_Y$, let $U\subseteq X$ be a nonempty admissible truth set, and let $F:U\to Y$ be a forward map. Choose a Borel set $D\in\mathcal B(X)$ with $D\subseteq U$ such that the restriction $G:=F|_D:D\to Y$ is measurable for the trace Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal B(D):=\{D\cap A:A\in\mathcal B(X)\}$. A prior on this forward domain is a Borel probability measure $\mu$ on $X$ such that $\mu(D)=1$. Its restriction $\mu|_D$, defined by $\mu|_D(A)=\mu(A)$ for $A\in\mathcal B(D)$, is then a probability measure on $D$, and the induced data law is $G_\#(\mu|_D)$, defined by $G_\#(\mu|_D)(E)=(\mu|_D)(G^{-1}(E))$ for $E\in\Sigma_Y$. A Borel probability on $X$ with $\mu(D)<1$ is not a prior on this declared forward domain.

Let $X$ be a separable real Banach space with its norm topology, $D\subseteq X$ a Borel forward-map domain, and $\mu_0$ a Borel probability measure on $X$ with $\mu_0(D)=1$. Write $\mu_{0,D}$ for its restriction to $D$, so $\mu_{0,D}(A)=\mu_0(A)$ for $A\in\mathcal B(D):=\{D\cap B:B\in\mathcal B(X)\}$. Let $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ be a measurable data space. A likelihood potential is a function $\Phi:D\times\mathsf Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ that is measurable from $\bigl(D\times\mathsf Y,\mathcal B(D)\otimes\mathcal Y\bigr)$ to $\bigl((-\infty,+\infty],\mathcal B((-\infty,+\infty])\bigr)$, where $\mathcal B((-\infty,+\infty])$ is the trace of $\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$ on $(-\infty,+\infty]$. Viewing $\Phi$ via the inclusion $(-\infty,+\infty]\hookrightarrow\overline{\mathbb R}$, it is also product-measurable as an extended-real-valued map because for every Borel set $B\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$, $\Phi^{-1}(B)=\Phi^{-1}(B\cap(-\infty,+\infty])$ is measurable by the definition of the trace sigma-algebra. Here $+\infty$ is allowed and $-\infty$ is excluded; set $e^{-\infty}=0$. The scalar map $t\mapsto e^{-t}$ on this range is continuous at finite $t$, and is continuous at $+\infty$: given $\varepsilon>0$, the limit supplies $a\in\mathbb R$ such that $t>a$ implies $e^{-t}<\varepsilon$, and the order-topology neighborhood $(a,+\infty]$ maps into $[0,\varepsilon)$. Hence it is Borel, so $L_\Phi:D\times\mathsf Y\to[0,+\infty)$, $L_\Phi(u;y):=e^{-\Phi(u;y)}$, is product-measurable by composition, and each section $u\mapsto L_\Phi(u;y)$ is nonnegative and measurable. Define its evidence by
$$
Z_\Phi(y):=\int_D L_\Phi(u;y)\,\mu_{0,D}(du)\in[0,+\infty].
$$
For each fixed $y$ with $0<Z_\Phi(y)<+\infty$, define the normalized fiberwise update on $A\in\mathcal B(D)$ by
$$\Pi^y(A):=\frac{\int_A L_\Phi(u;y)\,\mu_{0,D}(du)}{Z_\Phi(y)}.$$
No normalized fiberwise update is defined by this formula when $Z_\Phi(y)=0$ or $Z_\Phi(y)=+\infty$.

For a data-indexed claim, an observation model and its version convention must also be specified. Let $X$ be a separable real Banach space with norm $\|\cdot\|_X$, let $D\subseteq X$ be Borel, and let $\mu_0$ be a Borel probability on $X$ with $\mu_0(D)=1$. Give $D$ the relative topology and Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal B(D)=\{D\cap B:B\in\mathcal B(X)\}$, and let $\mu_{0,D}$ be the restriction of $\mu_0$ to $D$, so $\mu_{0,D}(A)=\mu_0(A)$ for $A\in\mathcal B(D)$. $$
\Phi(u;y)\ge -M_1(\|u\|_X)\quad(u\in D,\ y\in\mathsf Y_0),\qquad

$$

law on a real separable Banach
space $B$, and let $H\subseteq B$ be its covariance RKHS. Define
$\operatorname{supp}\mu$ to be the set of $x\in B$ for which every open
neighborhood has positive $\mu$-measure. Then
$$\operatorname{supp}\mu=\overline H^{\,B}.$$

$$C\ell=E[\ell(W)W]\in B,\qquad Q(\ell,m)=E[\ell(W)m(W)]\quad(\ell,m\in B^*).$$
The **Cameron–Martin reproducing-kernel Hilbert space** $H$ is the completion
of $B^*/N$ in the inner product induced by $Q$, where
$N=\{\ell\in B^*:Q(\ell,\ell)=0\}$. The canonical map sends the class of

$\|\cdot\|_H$. The preceding construction is well-defined by
[[thm-banach-gaussian-covariance-rkhs-is-well-defined]].

inside $B$; it is not the space of all continuous functions on an arbitrary
index set.

Assume AC. Under the hypotheses and notation of

Assume the Axiom of Choice, the Hahn–Banach theorem, and countable choice. Let $B$ be a real separable Banach space, and let $W$ be a centered Borel Gaussian random element with law $\mu$. $$ \frac{\mu(\overline B_B(ih_1,r))}{\mu(\overline B_B(ih_2,r))} \longrightarrow \exp\!\left(\frac{\|h_2\|_E^2-\|h_1\|_E^2}{2}\right) \qquad(r\downarrow0). $$
The denominator is positive for every $r>0$.

Let $B$ be a separable Banach space with norm $\|\cdot\|_B$, and let $\Pi$ be a Borel probability measure on $B$. For $z\in B$ and $r>0$, write $\overline B_B(z,r)=\{u\in B:\|u-z\|_B\le r\}$ and $m_r(z)=\Pi(\overline B_B(z,r))$. A **strong small-ball MAP** is a point $z\in B$ for which
$$ \frac{m_r(z)}{\sup_{x\in B}m_r(x)}\longrightarrow1\qquad(r\downarrow0). $$
Assume AC for the covariance-induced Cameron–Martin notation. If $\Pi$ is a posterior law formed by weighting a centered Gaussian prior $\Pi_0$ on $B$, let $C\ell=\int_B\ell(u)u\,\Pi_0(du)$ be its covariance operator and let $E$ be the completion of $B^*/\ker C$ with inner product $\langle[\ell],[m]\rangle_E=m(C\ell)$; the canonical injection $i:E\to B$ extends $[\ell]\mapsto C\ell$. $$ \lim_{r\downarrow0}\frac{m_r(ih)}{m_r(ik)} $$
exists and is at least $1$. This pairwise comparison over fixed Cameron–Martin centers does not assert the global strong small-ball MAP condition.

For every $r>0$, $\sup_{x\in B}m_r(x)>0$: a countable dense subset gives a countable cover of $B$ by radius-$r$ open balls, each contained in its corresponding closed ball, and countable subadditivity rules out all such closed balls having zero probability.

Every bounded sequence of reals has a convergent subsequence: if $(x_k)$ is a
sequence of reals and there is $M \in \mathbb{R}$ with $|x_k| \le M$ for every
$k \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-sequence]]), then there is a strictly increasing
$n : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and a real $L$ with $x_{n_j} \to L$.

Equivalently: the subsequential limit set of a bounded sequence is nonempty
([[def-subsequential-limit]]).

The theorem is the exact repair of the false claim that a bounded sequence
converges. A bounded
sequence need not converge, and the alternating sequence is the standing witness;
what boundedness does force is that *some* subsequence converges. The converse of
the theorem is false, and badly so: a sequence with a convergent subsequence need
not be bounded.

Choose $0<\varepsilon<a$ with $a$ from [F3]. The lower bound gives $\Phi(u)\ge M_\varepsilon-\varepsilon\|u\|_B^2$. Define the nonnegative Borel function $M_1(t)=\max\{0,\varepsilon t^2-M_\varepsilon\}$. Then $\Phi(u)\ge-M_1(\|u\|_B)$ and
$$ e^{M_1(\|u\|_B)} \le 1+e^{-M_\varepsilon}e^{\varepsilon\|u\|_B^2}. $$
The right side is $\mu$-integrable by [F3]. Since $\Phi$ is locally Lipschitz it is finite and continuous on $B$. Apply [F2] with the single datum and $D=B$; the prior definition in [F1] makes $\mu$ a prior on $B$. Thus $0<Z<\infty$ and $\Pi$ is a probability.

Fix $h\in E$. Local Lipschitz continuity at $ih$ supplies constants $L_h<\infty$ and $\rho_h>0$ such that $|\Phi(u)-\Phi(ih)|\le L_h r$ whenever $\|u-ih\|_B\le r<\rho_h$. Therefore
$$ e^{-\Phi(ih)-L_hr}\mu(\overline B_B(ih,r)) \le \int_{\overline B_B(ih,r)}e^{-\Phi(u)}\,\mu(du) \le e^{-\Phi(ih)+L_hr}\mu(\overline B_B(ih,r)). $$
For fixed $h_1,h_2\in E$, divide the two integral bounds and cancel the common normalizer $Z$ in [F1]. The factors from the Lipschitz errors tend to $1$, and [F7] gives
$$ \frac{\Pi(\overline B_B(ih_1,r))}{\Pi(\overline B_B(ih_2,r))} \longrightarrow e^{\Phi(ih_2)-\Phi(ih_1)} e^{(\|h_2\|_E^2-\|h_1\|_E^2)/2} =e^{I(ih_2)-I(ih_1)}. $$
The denominator is positive for small $r$: [F4] gives positive prior mass to every open ball about $ih_2$ (since $ih_2\in iE$), and the likelihood is strictly positive and continuous there.

Let $C_i=\|i:E\to B\|$. If $E=\{0\}$, $I$ has the sole candidate $0$ and is minimized there. Otherwise $C_i>0$. Choose $\varepsilon<1/(4C_i^2)$ and use the potential lower bound to obtain, for every $h\in E$,
$$ I(ih)\ge M_\varepsilon+\frac12\|h\|_E^2-\varepsilon\|ih\|_B^2 \ge M_\varepsilon+\frac14\|h\|_E^2. $$
Since $I(0)=\Phi(0)$ is finite, $\inf_E I$ is finite and any minimizing sequence is bounded in $E$.

Choose a minimizing sequence $(h_n)$ in $E$ and, by [F9], pass to a subsequence for which $\|h_n\|_E\to L$. Its images lie in a fixed multiple of the closed $E$-unit ball, whose image is compact in $B$ by [F6]. Pass to a further subsequence with $ih_n\to v$ in $B$; compactness means $v=ih$ for some $h\in E$. For each $\ell\in B^*$, [F5] gives
$$ |\ell(ih)|=\lim_n|\ell(ih_n)| =\lim_n|\langle h_n,[\ell]\rangle_E| \le L\|[\ell]\|_E. $$
The classes $[\ell]$ are dense in $E$ by [F5]. For every unit $g\in E$, choose nonzero classes $[\ell_n]\to g$ and normalize them; then $[\ell_n]/\|[\ell_n]\|_E\to g$. Thus the normalized covariance classes are dense in the unit sphere, and the supremum of $|\langle h,[\ell]\rangle_E|$ over them is $\|h\|_E$. The displayed bound gives $\|h\|_E\le L$. $$ I(ih)\le\lim_n\left(\Phi(ih_n)+\frac12\|h_n\|_E^2\right)=\inf_E I. $$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume AC. Let $d\ge1$, $m\in\mathbb R^d$, and let $\Sigma$ be a real symmetric positive-definite $d\times d$ matrix. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then its law has Lebesgue density
$$f_{m,\Sigma}(x)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}\det(\Sigma)^{-1/2} \exp\!\left(-\tfrac12(x-m)^T\Sigma^{-1}(x-m)\right), \qquad x\in\mathbb R^d.$$

Let $X$ be a separable real Banach space with its norm topology, $D\subseteq X$ a Borel forward-map domain, and $\mu_0$ a Borel probability measure on $X$ with $\mu_0(D)=1$. Write $\mu_{0,D}$ for its restriction to $D$, so $\mu_{0,D}(A)=\mu_0(A)$ for $A\in\mathcal B(D):=\{D\cap B:B\in\mathcal B(X)\}$. Let $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ be a measurable data space. A likelihood potential is a function $\Phi:D\times\mathsf Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ that is measurable from $\bigl(D\times\mathsf Y,\mathcal B(D)\otimes\mathcal Y\bigr)$ to $\bigl((-\infty,+\infty],\mathcal B((-\infty,+\infty])\bigr)$, where $\mathcal B((-\infty,+\infty])$ is the trace of $\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$ on $(-\infty,+\infty]$. Viewing $\Phi$ via the inclusion $(-\infty,+\infty]\hookrightarrow\overline{\mathbb R}$, it is also product-measurable as an extended-real-valued map because for every Borel set $B\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$, $\Phi^{-1}(B)=\Phi^{-1}(B\cap(-\infty,+\infty])$ is measurable by the definition of the trace sigma-algebra. Here $+\infty$ is allowed and $-\infty$ is excluded; set $e^{-\infty}=0$. The scalar map $t\mapsto e^{-t}$ on this range is continuous at finite $t$, and is continuous at $+\infty$: given $\varepsilon>0$, the limit supplies $a\in\mathbb R$ such that $t>a$ implies $e^{-t}<\varepsilon$, and the order-topology neighborhood $(a,+\infty]$ maps into $[0,\varepsilon)$. Hence it is Borel, so $L_\Phi:D\times\mathsf Y\to[0,+\infty)$, $L_\Phi(u;y):=e^{-\Phi(u;y)}$, is product-measurable by composition, and each section $u\mapsto L_\Phi(u;y)$ is nonnegative and measurable. Define its evidence by
$$
Z_\Phi(y):=\int_D L_\Phi(u;y)\,\mu_{0,D}(du)\in[0,+\infty].
$$
For each fixed $y$ with $0<Z_\Phi(y)<+\infty$, define the normalized fiberwise update on $A\in\mathcal B(D)$ by
$$\Pi^y(A):=\frac{\int_A L_\Phi(u;y)\,\mu_{0,D}(du)}{Z_\Phi(y)}.$$
No normalized fiberwise update is defined by this formula when $Z_\Phi(y)=0$ or $Z_\Phi(y)=+\infty$.

For a data-indexed claim, an observation model and its version convention must also be specified. In the dominated case, let $Q$ be a proper probability kernel from $(D,\mathcal B(D))$ to $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$, let $\nu$ be a sigma-finite measure on $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$, and suppose $Q(u,B)=\int_B L_\Phi(u;y)\,\nu(dy)$ for every $u\in D$ and $B\in\mathcal Y$. Then $Z_\Phi$ is the density of the prior-predictive data law with respect to $\nu$; a data-indexed conditional-law version uses $\Pi^y$ when $0<Z_\Phi(y)<\infty$ and the prior $\mu_{0,D}$ when $Z_\Phi(y)$ is zero or infinite. These filled fibers have zero prior-predictive mass, and their chosen values are not normalized fiberwise updates. More generally, for a proper Bayesian model with standard-Borel parameter space $(D,\mathcal B(D))$ and data space $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ (each measurably isomorphic to the Borel space of a Polish space), the Axiom of Choice guarantees a data-indexed posterior kernel; its values are unique as probability measures outside one data-marginal-null set, and values on that null set remain version choices. The dominated construction is choice-free; the separate standard-Borel existence branch assumes the Axiom of Choice.

Assume AC. Let $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$ with positive-definite covariance
$\Sigma$. Let $L:\mathbb R^d\to[0,M]$ be Borel measurable and symmetric,
$L(-x)=L(x)$, and quasi-convex, meaning each sublevel set
$\{x:L(x)\le t\}$ is convex. Then for every $a\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$E L(X-a)\ge E L(X-m).$$
Thus the Gaussian center $m$ minimizes expected loss. The result includes
quasi-convex losses whose sublevel sets are not closed.

Let $B$ be a separable Banach space with norm $\|\cdot\|_B$, and let $\Pi$ be a Borel probability measure on $B$. For $z\in B$ and $r>0$, write $\overline B_B(z,r)=\{u\in B:\|u-z\|_B\le r\}$ and $m_r(z)=\Pi(\overline B_B(z,r))$. A **strong small-ball MAP** is a point $z\in B$ for which
$$ \frac{m_r(z)}{\sup_{x\in B}m_r(x)}\longrightarrow1\qquad(r\downarrow0). $$
Assume AC for the covariance-induced Cameron–Martin notation. If $\Pi$ is a posterior law formed by weighting a centered Gaussian prior $\Pi_0$ on $B$, let $C\ell=\int_B\ell(u)u\,\Pi_0(du)$ be its covariance operator and let $E$ be the completion of $B^*/\ker C$ with inner product $\langle[\ell],[m]\rangle_E=m(C\ell)$; the canonical injection $i:E\to B$ extends $[\ell]\mapsto C\ell$. A **Cameron–Martin ratio mode** is a point $ih\in iE$ such that, for every $k\in E$, the denominator is positive for all sufficiently small $r$ and
$$ \lim_{r\downarrow0}\frac{m_r(ih)}{m_r(ik)} $$
exists and is at least $1$. This pairwise comparison over fixed Cameron–Martin centers does not assert the global strong small-ball MAP condition.

For every $r>0$, $\sup_{x\in B}m_r(x)>0$: a countable dense subset gives a countable cover of $B$ by radius-$r$ open balls, each contained in its corresponding closed ball, and countable subadditivity rules out all such closed balls having zero probability.

Let $n \ge 1$, let $h \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and let $E + h$ be the translate of
$E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-translation-of-a-set-in-rn]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n^*(E+h) = \lambda_n^*(E)$ for **every** subset $E$;
2. $E$ is Lebesgue measurable if and only if $E+h$ is;
3. $\lambda_n(E+h) = \lambda_n(E)$ for every Lebesgue measurable $E$.

**No choice principle is used.** Lebesgue outer measure is defined as an infimum
and the Carathéodory condition is a family of equations between its values, so
all three clauses are statements about objects that exist in ZF; countable
choice is needed to know that $\lambda_n$ is a measure, not to know that it is
translation invariant.

derivations.claim: By [F1], the prior and noise have positive Gaussian densities proportional to $\exp(-\tfrac12u^TC^{-1}u)$ and $\exp(-\tfrac12(y-Au)^T\Gamma^{-1}(y-Au))$, respectively. For any $w$, $w^T\Gamma^{-1}w\ge0$: write $w=\Gamma v$, so $w^T\Gamma^{-1}w=v^T\Gamma v\ge0$. Thus $\Phi_y\ge0$ and $e^{-\Phi_y}\le1$, so the evidence is finite. It is positive because $\Phi_y$ is continuous and finite at $0$, hence $e^{-\Phi_y}$ is bounded below by a positive constant on a sufficiently small ball about $0$, and the prior density in [F1] gives that ball positive mass. The posterior update [F1] is therefore defined. Its Lebesgue density is proportional to the product of the prior density and likelihood, hence to $e^{-I_y(u)}$. Put $Q=C^{-1}+A^T\Gamma^{-1}A$. For $v\ne0$, $v^TQv=v^TC^{-1}v+(Av)^T\Gamma^{-1}(Av)>0$: if $z=C^{-1}v$, then $v^TC^{-1}v=z^TCz>0$, and the second term is nonnegative by the preceding argument. Thus $Q$ is positive definite. Completing the square gives the unique minimizer $m=Q^{-1}A^T\Gamma^{-1}y$, and the posterior is the nondegenerate Gaussian $N(m,Q^{-1})$.

For every $r>0$, apply [F2] to this posterior and the loss $L_r(x)=\mathbf1_{\{\|x\|_2>r\}}$. Its sublevel sets are the closed radius-$r$ ball and the whole space, so it is bounded, symmetric and quasi-convex. Thus every ball of radius $r$ has posterior mass at most the ball centered at $m$, and the supremum in [F3] is attained at $m$. Consequently $m$ is a strong small-ball MAP.

Let $q$ be the positive continuous posterior density. For any fixed $z\in\mathbb R^d$, the absolute difference between $|B_r|^{-1}\Pi(B_r(z))$ and $q(z)$ is at most $\sup_{\|x-z\|_2\le r}|q(x)-q(z)|$, which tends to zero by continuity. The same holds at any $v$, and [F4] makes the ball volumes equal; hence $\Pi(B_r(z))/\Pi(B_r(v))\to q(z)/q(v)$. Since $q$ is proportional to $e^{-I_y}$, the finite-dimensional small-ball ratio agrees with the density and Onsager–Machlup comparison.

there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $H_0$ and $H_1$ be separable real Hilbert spaces with a continuous inclusion $H_1\hookrightarrow H_0$. Let $(e_j)_{j\ge1}$ be an orthonormal basis of $H_0$ that is a complete orthogonal basis of $H_1$, write $w_j=\|e_j\|_{H_1}^2>0$, and set $f_j=e_j/\sqrt{w_j}$, so $(f_j)_{j\ge1}$ is an orthonormal basis of $H_1$. Let $(\xi_j)_{j\ge1}$ be independent real random variables on one probability space with $\mathbb E\xi_j=0$ and $\mathbb E\xi_j^2=1$, and let $\lambda_j\ge0$ satisfy $\sum_{j\ge1}\lambda_jw_j<\infty$. Then
$$S_N=\sum_{j=1}^N\sqrt{\lambda_j}\,\xi_j e_j$$
converges almost surely in $H_1$ and in $L^2(\Omega;H_1)$ to an $H_1$-valued Borel-measurable random element $S$, with
$$\mathbb E\|S\|_{H_1}^2=\sum_{j\ge1}\lambda_jw_j.$$
These norm-convergence conclusions use no choice axiom beyond the supplied probability space and variables. For the following Gaussian conclusions, assume in addition that each $\xi_j$ has the standard normal law $N(0,1)$. Under the Axiom of Choice and countable choice, $S$ is a centered Borel Gaussian random element in $H_1$. Its covariance map $C:H_1^*\to H_1$, transported to $H_1$ by the Hilbert-space Riesz identification, is diagonal in the basis $(f_j)_{j\ge1}$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_jw_j$, and these eigenvalues are summable. If $D$ is a Borel forward-map domain in $H_1$ and $\mathbb P(S\in D)=1$, then the law of $S$ is a prior on $D$. Under the Axiom of Choice there is $a>0$ such that
$$\mathbb E\exp\!\bigl(a\|S\|_{H_1}^2\bigr)<\infty.$$

Let $X$ be a set and let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]). A **measure** on $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a function

$$\mu:\mathcal A\longrightarrow[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$$

such that:

1. $\mu(\varnothing)=0$;
2. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$,
   $$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k),$$
   where the right side is the nonnegative extended sum of [[def-nonnegative-extended-series]].

The second condition is **countable additivity**. It begins at index $0$ and includes the case in which some term or the total sum is $+\infty$.

Let $\mu$ be a measure and let $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ be measurable. Then

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ one also has

including $m=0$, where both sides are $0$.

The finite sums telescope as $\sum_{j=1}^N\lambda_j=\sum_{j=1}^N(1/j-1/(j+1))=1-1/(N+1)\le1$, so the required infinite sum is finite. Thus [F1] applies to the stated independent standard normals and proves that $W$ is a centered Borel Gaussian random element.

Suppose that $\lambda$ is a translation-invariant Borel measure finite on every bounded Borel set. Put $U_j=\{x:\|x-e_j\|_2<1/3\}$. For $j\ne k$, $\|e_j-e_k\|_2=\sqrt2>2/3$, so the $U_j$ are pairwise disjoint. Each lies in the bounded ball $\{x:\|x\|_2<2\}$ by the triangle inequality. Translation invariance gives $\lambda(U_j)=m$ independent of $j$. If $m>0$, the first $N$ disjoint balls have total measure $Nm$ for every $N$, contradicting finiteness of the radius-two ball. Hence $m=0$.

Translation invariance and step 2.1 make every radius-$1/3$ ball have measure zero. Let $D$ be the set of finitely supported rational sequences. [F3] makes $D$ countable: it is the countable union, over support lengths $N$, of the countable set $\mathbb Q^N$ padded with zeros. It is dense in $\ell^2$: for any $x\in\ell^2$ and $\epsilon>0$, choose $N$ so that the squared tail sum is less than $\epsilon^2/4$, then approximate the first $N$ coordinates by rationals with squared total error less than $\epsilon^2/4$; the resulting padded vector is within $\epsilon$ of $x$. The radius-$1/3$ balls centered at $D$ therefore form a countable cover of $\ell^2$. By [F2], $\lambda(\ell^2)=0$, and [F4] makes every Borel subset null. This contradicts that $\lambda$ is nonzero. Hence no such reference measure exists, refuting the statement; in particular, the displayed Gaussian has no density relative to one.

Let $X$ be a separable real Banach space with its norm topology, $D\subseteq X$ a Borel forward-map domain, and $\mu_0$ a Borel probability measure on $X$ with $\mu_0(D)=1$. Write $\mu_{0,D}$ for its restriction to $D$, so $\mu_{0,D}(A)=\mu_0(A)$ for $A\in\mathcal B(D):=\{D\cap B:B\in\mathcal B(X)\}$. Let $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ be a measurable data space. A likelihood potential is a function $\Phi:D\times\mathsf Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ that is measurable from $\bigl(D\times\mathsf Y,\mathcal B(D)\otimes\mathcal Y\bigr)$ to $\bigl((-\infty,+\infty],\mathcal B((-\infty,+\infty])\bigr)$, where $\mathcal B((-\infty,+\infty])$ is the trace of $\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$ on $(-\infty,+\infty]$. Viewing $\Phi$ via the inclusion $(-\infty,+\infty]\hookrightarrow\overline{\mathbb R}$, it is also product-measurable as an extended-real-valued map because for every Borel set $B\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$, $\Phi^{-1}(B)=\Phi^{-1}(B\cap(-\infty,+\infty])$ is measurable by the definition of the trace sigma-algebra. Here $+\infty$ is allowed and $-\infty$ is excluded; set $e^{-\infty}=0$. The scalar map $t\mapsto e^{-t}$ on this range is continuous at finite $t$, and is continuous at $+\infty$: given $\varepsilon>0$, the limit supplies $a\in\mathbb R$ such that $t>a$ implies $e^{-t}<\varepsilon$, and the order-topology neighborhood $(a,+\infty]$ maps into $[0,\varepsilon)$. Hence it is Borel, so $L_\Phi:D\times\mathsf Y\to[0,+\infty)$, $L_\Phi(u;y):=e^{-\Phi(u;y)}$, is product-measurable by composition, and each section $u\mapsto L_\Phi(u;y)$ is nonnegative and measurable. Define its evidence by
$$
Z_\Phi(y):=\int_D L_\Phi(u;y)\,\mu_{0,D}(du)\in[0,+\infty].
$$
For each fixed $y$ with $0<Z_\Phi(y)<+\infty$, define the normalized fiberwise update on $A\in\mathcal B(D)$ by
$$\Pi^y(A):=\frac{\int_A L_\Phi(u;y)\,\mu_{0,D}(du)}{Z_\Phi(y)}.$$
No normalized fiberwise update is defined by this formula when $Z_\Phi(y)=0$ or $Z_\Phi(y)=+\infty$.

For a data-indexed claim, an observation model and its version convention must also be specified. In the dominated case, let $Q$ be a proper probability kernel from $(D,\mathcal B(D))$ to $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$, let $\nu$ be a sigma-finite measure on $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$, and suppose $Q(u,B)=\int_B L_\Phi(u;y)\,\nu(dy)$ for every $u\in D$ and $B\in\mathcal Y$. Then $Z_\Phi$ is the density of the prior-predictive data law with respect to $\nu$; a data-indexed conditional-law version uses $\Pi^y$ when $0<Z_\Phi(y)<\infty$ and the prior $\mu_{0,D}$ when $Z_\Phi(y)$ is zero or infinite. These filled fibers have zero prior-predictive mass, and their chosen values are not normalized fiberwise updates. More generally, for a proper Bayesian model with standard-Borel parameter space $(D,\mathcal B(D))$ and data space $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ (each measurably isomorphic to the Borel space of a Polish space), the Axiom of Choice guarantees a data-indexed posterior kernel; its values are unique as probability measures outside one data-marginal-null set, and values on that null set remain version choices. The dominated construction is choice-free; the separate standard-Borel existence branch assumes the Axiom of Choice.

Let $B$ be a separable Banach space with norm $\|\cdot\|_B$, and let $\Pi$ be a Borel probability measure on $B$. For $z\in B$ and $r>0$, write $\overline B_B(z,r)=\{u\in B:\|u-z\|_B\le r\}$ and $m_r(z)=\Pi(\overline B_B(z,r))$. A **strong small-ball MAP** is a point $z\in B$ for which
$$ \frac{m_r(z)}{\sup_{x\in B}m_r(x)}\longrightarrow1\qquad(r\downarrow0). $$
Assume AC for the covariance-induced Cameron–Martin notation. If $\Pi$ is a posterior law formed by weighting a centered Gaussian prior $\Pi_0$ on $B$, let $C\ell=\int_B\ell(u)u\,\Pi_0(du)$ be its covariance operator and let $E$ be the completion of $B^*/\ker C$ with inner product $\langle[\ell],[m]\rangle_E=m(C\ell)$; the canonical injection $i:E\to B$ extends $[\ell]\mapsto C\ell$. A **Cameron–Martin ratio mode** is a point $ih\in iE$ such that, for every $k\in E$, the denominator is positive for all sufficiently small $r$ and
$$ \lim_{r\downarrow0}\frac{m_r(ih)}{m_r(ik)} $$
exists and is at least $1$. This pairwise comparison over fixed Cameron–Martin centers does not assert the global strong small-ball MAP condition.

For every $r>0$, $\sup_{x\in B}m_r(x)>0$: a countable dense subset gives a countable cover of $B$ by radius-$r$ open balls, each contained in its corresponding closed ball, and countable subadditivity rules out all such closed balls having zero probability.

Fix $n \ge 1$ and let $\lambda_n^*$ be the Lebesgue outer set function on $\mathbb{R}^n$
([[def-lebesgue-outer-measure]]). A set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is
**Lebesgue measurable** when

$$\lambda_n^*(A) \;=\; \lambda_n^*(A \cap E) \;+\; \lambda_n^*(A \setminus E) \qquad \text{for every } A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n .$$

This formula makes sense before any outer-measure theorem is invoked. Under
countable choice, [[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-is-an-outer-measure-agreeing-with-volume]]
makes $\lambda_n^*$ an outer measure, and the displayed condition is then exactly
Carathéodory measurability in the sense of [[def-caratheodory-measurable-set]].

The family of Lebesgue measurable sets is written $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$,
and **Lebesgue measure** is the restriction

$$\lambda_n \;:=\; \lambda_n^*\!\restriction_{\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)} .$$

On the real line the subscript is dropped and $\lambda := \lambda_1$.

The quantifier over every test set $A$ is part of the condition, and no
hypothesis on $E$ is imposed before it is tested. That
$\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra and that $\lambda_n$ is a complete
measure on it are not part of this definition: they are proved, under the Axiom
of Countable Choice, in [[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]], which is
recorded in this item's `justified_by` because it is a statement about the
objects introduced here. Until that theorem the symbols $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$
and $\lambda_n$ name a family of sets and a restricted set function, nothing more.

On $[0,1]$, $p(\theta)=\theta^2(1-\theta)\ge0$. Its derivative is $p'(\theta)=\theta(2-3\theta)$, so its maximum is $p(2/3)=4/27<1$. Therefore $p$ and $1-p$ define valid conditional probabilities for $Y=1$ and $Y=0$. By [F3], the evidence for $Y=1$ is
$$ Z=\int_0^1\theta^2(1-\theta)\,d\theta=\frac13-\frac14=\frac1{12}>0. $$
The posterior formula [F1] gives density $q(\theta)=12\theta^2(1-\theta)$ on $[0,1]$, extended by zero on $\mathbb R\setminus[0,1]$.

On $(0,1)$, $q'(\theta)=12\theta(2-3\theta)$, so $q$ increases up to $2/3$ and decreases after it; $q(0)=q(1)=0$. Thus $q_{\max}=q(2/3)>0$ is the unique density maximum. For any center $x\in\mathbb R$ and $r>0$, [F3] gives $m_r(x)\le2r q_{\max}$. For $0<r<1/3$, the interval $[2/3-r,2/3+r]$ lies inside $[0,1]$, and continuity of $q$ gives $m_r(2/3)/(2r)\to q_{\max}$. Hence
$$ 1\ge\frac{m_r(2/3)}{\sup_{x\in\mathbb R}m_r(x)} \ge\frac{m_r(2/3)}{2r q_{\max}}\longrightarrow1. $$
By [F2], $2/3$ is a strong small-ball MAP.

The posterior mean is
$$ \int_0^1\theta q(\theta)\,d\theta =12\int_0^1(\theta^3-\theta^4)\,d\theta =12\left(\frac14-\frac15\right)=\frac35. $$
Since $3/5\ne2/3$, the posterior mean differs from the strong small-ball MAP.
